meaning: Mother; epithet of Pārvatī/Durgā, the multi-armed goddess with lion

phonemes.desc: Short a plus labial nasal m, a soft opening.
Voiced labial stop plus short i.
Voiceless velar stop plus long ā, the feminine ending.

pronunciation.approximation: 'um-bee-KAH' — the final syllable is long and carries the weight of the name.
pronunciation.note: Ambikā means literally 'little mother' or 'dear mother', an affectionate epithet that became a name of the Goddess in her protective, warrior form.

domains.title: The Divine Mother Armed
domains.subtitle: Motherhood, Power, and the Protection of the Cosmos
domains.lead: Ambikā is the Mother who takes up arms. As an epithet of Pārvatī and Durgā, she is the gentle parent become warrioress: multi-armed, riding or attended by a lion, and invoked against the demons who threaten cosmic order. Her name means 'mother', but in cult it means 'mother who fights for her children'.

cards.name: Divine Motherhood
cards.desc: The maternal face of the Goddess, compassionate and inexhaustible.

cards.name: Warrior Protection
cards.desc: She wields weapons against demons to defend devotees and restore dharma.

cards.name: The Lion
cards.desc: Her vehicle and symbol of sovereign, ferocious maternal power.

cards.name: Multi-Armed Might
cards.desc: Each arm carries a divine weapon gifted by the gods for the destruction of evil.

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Vehicle and emblem of royal, wrathful maternal power

symbols.name: Trident (trishūla)
symbols.meaning: Śiva's weapon, here the Mother's power to destroy ignorance and evil

symbols.name: Lotus
symbols.meaning: Purity unfolding even from the battlefield of existence

symbols.name: Multiple arms
symbols.meaning: The many powers of the gods concentrated in one protective form

mythology.lead: Ambikā's mythology is not separate from that of Pārvatī and Durgā; it is one mask of the Great Goddess, the one who becomes a mother to the cosmos and a warrior to its enemies.

myths.title: Ambikā as Pārvatī
myths.text: In the Shiva Purana, Pārvatī is called Ambikā when she appears as the divine consort and mother. The name softens her into maternal affection, yet the same goddess can assume the ten-armed form of Durgā when demons threaten the gods.

myths.title: The Slayer of Demons
myths.text: When the buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura overthrows the gods, the Goddess emerges from the combined tejas of the gods. As Ambikā/Durgā she rides a lion and destroys the armies of demons, restoring cosmic order through martial motherhood.

myths.title: Worship across India
myths.text: Ambikā is worshipped in temples across Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra, often as a local guardian goddess and healer. Her shrines are frequented by women seeking protection for children and family.

lore.syncretism: Ambikā is not distinct from Pārvatī, Durgā, Umā, or Gaurī; she is one grammatical and theological inflection of the Great Goddess (Mahādevī). The epithet emphasizes motherhood, while Durgā emphasizes fortress-like protection and Kālī emphasizes time and destruction. In tantric and devotional contexts these are understood as modes of a single divine power rather than separate goddesses.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name Ambikā remains a common epithet for the Goddess in Hindu devotion, temple names, and personal names across South Asia and the diaspora. As an emblem of armed motherhood, she resonates with modern movements that frame women's power as protective rather than merely aggressive. Her lion-riding, multi-armed image is one of the most recognizable icons of Hindu goddess worship worldwide.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ambikā teaches that motherhood is not passive. In her, the womb and the weapon are not opposites but complements: the same love that gives birth will destroy anything that threatens the child. This is not a sentimental goddess; she is a sovereign parent whose tenderness has teeth.

For the devotee, Ambikā is the assurance that the cosmos has a mother, and that the mother is armed. She does not promise an end to struggle; she promises that the struggle is on the side of order, dharma, and life. To call on Ambikā is to remember that protection can be holy rage.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Sanskrit name is written in Devanagari as अम्बिका. The final long ā is marked by the macron in the Unicode restoration Ambikā, preserving the feminine nominative ending that the ASCII form drops.
